_meta.purpose: EU AI Act (2024/1689) in CatalogFile shape, so applyCatalogFile creates the framework, its requirements, the templates, their requirement links and the pack together.
_meta.why: Built inline in prisma/seed.ts, which is not run on production deploys. Extracted from a database seeded by that block, so the shape is carried over exactly rather than re-derived from grouping logic that ran at seed time.
_meta.grounding: Requirement codes, titles and sections, and the template titles, categories, frequencies and requirement links, are exactly those the inline block produced. Task content is NOT authored here — every template carries the generic five, as it did inline.

framework.name: EU AI Act (2024/1689)
framework.description: Risk-tiered AI regulation obligations (prohibited / high-risk / limited / GPAI / minimal).

metadata.copyright: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 is EU legislation in the public domain. Source: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj. Risk-tier classification is a tenant + legal-counsel decision; not legal advice.

requirements.title: Prohibited AI practices
requirements.summary: Do not place on the market, put into service, or use the AI practices banned by Article 5 (e.g. social scoring, untargeted facial-image scraping, manipulative or exploitative systems, certain biometric categorisation and real-time remote biometric identification).

requirements.title: Risk management system
requirements.summary: Establish, implement, document and maintain a risk management system across the high-risk AI system life cycle (Article 9).

requirements.title: Data and data governance
requirements.summary: Use training, validation and testing data sets that meet quality and governance criteria (Article 10).

requirements.title: Technical documentation
requirements.summary: Draw up and keep up to date the technical documentation demonstrating conformity (Article 11, Annex IV).

requirements.title: Record-keeping
requirements.summary: Design the system for automatic logging of events over its lifetime (Article 12).

requirements.title: Transparency and information to deployers
requirements.summary: Ensure operation is transparent enough for deployers to interpret output, with instructions for use (Article 13).

requirements.title: Human oversight
requirements.summary: Design the system so it can be effectively overseen by natural persons (Article 14).

requirements.title: Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
requirements.summary: Achieve appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, and perform consistently (Article 15).

requirements.title: Obligations of providers
requirements.summary: Meet the provider obligations for high-risk AI systems, including conformity assessment and CE marking (Article 16).

requirements.title: Quality management system
requirements.summary: Put a quality management system in place ensuring compliance (Article 17).

requirements.title: Obligations of deployers
requirements.summary: Meet deployer obligations: use per instructions, ensure human oversight, monitor operation (Article 26).

requirements.title: Fundamental rights impact assessment
requirements.summary: Perform a fundamental-rights impact assessment where required before deployment (Article 27).

requirements.title: Transparency obligations for certain AI systems
requirements.summary: Inform people they interact with an AI system, and label AI-generated or manipulated content (e.g. deepfakes) (Article 50).

requirements.title: Obligations for providers of GPAI models
requirements.summary: Maintain technical documentation, provide information to downstream providers, comply with copyright, and publish a training-content summary (Article 53).

requirements.title: Obligations for GPAI models with systemic risk
requirements.summary: For systemic-risk GPAI: model evaluation, adversarial testing, serious-incident tracking and reporting, and cybersecurity protection (Article 55).

requirements.title: Codes of conduct (voluntary)
requirements.summary: Minimal-risk systems carry no mandatory obligations; providers may adopt voluntary codes of conduct (Article 95).

templates.title: Prohibited AI practices
templates.description: Implements Art.5: know what every AI system in the organisation actually does, test each one against the practices the Act bans outright, and hold a dated record showing the organisation neither places them on the market, puts them into service nor uses them — together with a route that stops a system found to cross the line.

title.en: Catalogue every AI system in use and record what each one infers about a person

description.en: An absence can only be shown for systems somebody has written down, and the ones that matter here arrive without a procurement decision — a feature switched on inside a product already bought, a model a team wired into an internal tool, a capability a supplier added in an update. Record for each system what it does to or about people: what it infers, what it scores, what it decides, and whose data it runs on. The bans turn on behaviour rather than on product names, so a row reading 'HR analytics platform' and nothing else cannot be tested against any of them. Attach the catalogue with the date it was compiled and the name of whoever compiled it.

evidenceHint.en: AI system catalogue: one row per system giving its purpose, what it infers, scores or decides about people, and the population it runs on

text.en: Ask each department which AI features they use, including ones inside products already bought.
Add the models and AI features your own engineers built or wired into internal tools.
Record for each system what it infers, scores or decides about a person.
Name the population each system runs on: employees, students, customers, the public.
Mark the systems that arrive as a feature of something else, and name the supplier.
Date the catalogue and record who compiled it.

title.en: Write a yes-or-no test for each banned practice in terms a system can be checked against

description.en: The bans read as legal categories — scoring people from unrelated behaviour, scraping facial images untargeted, inferring emotion at work or in education, sorting people by sensitive characteristics from their biometrics — and a legal category cannot be answered by an engineer looking at a system. Turn each into a question about observable behaviour, with a yes, a no, and the facts that decide between them. Write the near-miss down too: the thing your organisation genuinely does that sits close to a line, and why it falls outside. Without the written test each assessment is one person's reading, nobody can review it, and two teams answer the same question differently. Attach the question set with the reasoning behind each boundary.

evidenceHint.en: Screening question set: one observable test per banned practice, the facts each answer turns on, and the near-miss cases worked through

text.en: Put each banned practice on its own line rather than in one paragraph.
Write each as a question about what the system does, answerable yes or no.
Record the facts an assessor must gather before answering each question.
Work through the near-miss cases the organisation actually operates.
Have whoever advises the organisation on the Act review the set, and date that review.

title.en: Establish who can stop a system that answers yes, and how long that takes

description.en: A screening question is only worth asking if a yes has somewhere to go. Name the person who can order a system switched off, the person who can refuse the purchase before it lands, and what happens between the answer and the shutdown — who is told, how affected teams keep working, and how a feature is disabled when the supplier owns the switch. Record how long each route actually takes, because a route that waits for a quarterly committee is not a stop. Decide as well what happens to what the system already produced: the scores already assigned, the records already written, the decisions already taken on them. Attach the written route with its named roles and its measured timings.

evidenceHint.en: Written stop-and-withdraw route: the roles that can trigger it, the steps from answer to shutdown, the measured time each takes, and the handling of outputs already produced

text.en: Name the role that can order an AI system taken out of use.
Write the steps between a yes answer and the system actually stopping.
Record how a supplier-controlled feature is disabled, and by whom.
Decide what happens to the outputs the system already produced.
Measure how long the route takes end to end and record the figure.

title.en: Run the screening questions across the catalogue and record an answer for every system

description.en: This is the recurring act that produces the evidence of absence. For each system in the catalogue record the answer to every screening question, who answered it, on what date, and what they looked at — the model documentation, the fields the system consumes, the decision its output feeds. The first run covers everything; later runs cover what was added or changed since, anything whose supplier shipped new capability, and a refresh of the systems touching employees, students or the public. A no with nothing behind it is the failure here, because it cannot be told apart from a question nobody asked. Attach the dated screening record for the period.

evidenceHint.en: Dated screening record for the period: every catalogued system against every banned-practice question, with the answer, the assessor and the evidence examined

text.en: Take the catalogue and the question set as they stand at the start of the run.
Record an answer, an assessor and a date for every system and question.
Note the evidence examined behind each answer, not the answer alone.
Answer in full every system added or changed since the last run.
Send any yes or unclear answer into the stop route without waiting for the run to end.
Close the run by dating the record and listing anything still unanswered.

title.en: Sample the systems answered no and check that answer against what they do today

description.en: A recorded no ages badly: a product adds emotion analytics in a release note, a score built for one purpose starts feeding a decision it was never built for, a pilot moves from customers to employees. Take a sample of the systems answered no, weighted towards those touching employees, students, the public or biometric data, and test the recorded answer against current behaviour — the outputs now produced, the fields now consumed, the decisions those outputs now feed. Where an answer no longer holds, correct it, send it into the stop route, and record how long the wrong answer stood, because that interval is the exposure. Attach the verification record with what was examined and what changed.

evidenceHint.en: Verification record naming the systems sampled, the evidence examined for each, the answers that changed and how long an incorrect answer had stood

text.en: Select a sample weighted towards systems that touch people directly.
Compare each recorded answer against what the system does today.
Read the supplier release notes issued since the answer was recorded.
Correct every answer that no longer holds and date the correction.
Record how long an incorrect answer stood before it was found.

templates.title: Risk management system for high-risk AI
templates.description: Implements Art.9: one high-risk AI system carries a risk file that runs the length of its life — the harms it can do to a person's health, safety or fundamental rights are identified against its intended purpose and its foreseeable misuse, each one is mitigated and the residual risk accepted by name, and what the field shows after release comes back into the file.

title.en: Define the intended purpose and foreseeable misuse this system's risk file is written against

description.en: Write down, for this one high-risk system, what it is built to do, where and on whom it will be used, and the uses it will foreseeably be put to that nobody intended — a triage model pointed at a population it was never validated on, an advisory score read as a decision, a tool used out of hours by staff who were never trained on it. Everything after this task is keyed to that statement: a risk nobody identified is almost always a use nobody wrote down, and a boundary naming only the intended purpose leaves the misuse half of the analysis with nothing to bite on. Name the system version the statement describes, because the same file applied to a retrained system is describing something else. Attach the dated scope statement.

evidenceHint.en: Dated scope statement for the system: intended purpose, deployment context, the people exposed to its output, the foreseeable misuses named, and the system version it describes

text.en: Name the single high-risk system and the version this file covers.
State the intended purpose in the terms the deployer is given.
List the uses the system will foreseeably be put to but is not built for.
Record who is exposed to the output, including people who never touch it.
Date the statement and hold it as the file's first content.

title.en: Identify and rate every harm this system can do to health, safety and fundamental rights

description.en: Work through the intended purpose and each foreseeable misuse and write down the harm that follows: a wrong output that delays treatment, a score that shuts somebody out of housing or work, a false match acted on before anybody checks it. One row per harm, naming who bears it — the risk that matters here falls on the person on the other side of the output, not on the organisation running the system, and a register that only counts legal and reputational exposure has analysed the wrong party. Rate each row and record the reasoning that produced the rating, because a bare score cannot be argued with later. Mark separately the harms that land on children or on people in vulnerable circumstances, whose exposure is not the average user's. Attach the risk register.

evidenceHint.en: Risk register for the system: one row per harm, giving the use it arises from, who bears it, the rating and the reasoning recorded behind that rating

text.en: Take each intended use and each misuse in turn and name the harm.
Write one row per harm, naming the people it falls on.
Rate each row and record the reasoning, not only the score.
Mark the harms that land on children or people in vulnerable circumstances.
Separate harm to the affected person from exposure to the organisation.

title.en: Select a mitigation for each rated risk and record the residual risk accepted before release

description.en: For every row above tolerance choose the measure that acts on it — a design change, a data change, a refusal path, a constraint on the operating conditions, instructions the deployer must follow — then set the threshold the measure has to reach and test it against the risk it was chosen for before the system goes out. A measure chosen but never tested against its own risk is an intention, and it reads identically to a working control once it is written in a table. Record what risk is left once the measure is in place and have a named person accept that remainder on a date, because residual risk nobody signed for is residual risk nobody owns. Attach the mitigation record with its test results and the acceptance.

evidenceHint.en: Mitigation record per risk row: the measure chosen, the threshold set beforehand, the test result against that threshold, the residual risk remaining, and the name and date of whoever accepted it

text.en: Choose a targeted measure for every risk above tolerance.
Set the threshold the measure must reach before any test is run.
Test the measure against the specific risk it was chosen for.
Record the risk that remains once the measure is in place.
Obtain a named acceptance of that remainder, dated before release.

title.en: Record the incidents, complaints and unexpected uses seen in the field against the risk file

description.en: Once the system is in use it will be given inputs, users and situations no design review imagined, and that is where the risks worth knowing about appear. Collect what comes back — incidents, deployer complaints, overrides by the people meant to oversee it, support tickets describing the system doing something surprising — and route each one into the file, either matched to an existing row or opened as a new one. The reports that match no row are the point of the task: they are the harms the identification missed, and they are invisible if the field feedback only ever reaches the support queue. Record the date each was seen and the date the file changed, so the lag between them can be read. Attach the field-feedback log for the period.

evidenceHint.en: Field-feedback log for the period: each incident, complaint, override and observed misuse with the risk row it was matched to or the new row opened, and the date it was seen beside the date the file changed

text.en: Collect incidents, complaints and overrides reported about the system.
Match each report to a risk row, or open a new row for it.
Flag the reports that match no risk anybody had identified.
Record the date seen beside the date the risk file was updated.

title.en: Reassess the risk file at planned intervals and after any change to the system or its use

description.en: A file written once before release and left alone is the ordinary failure of this control: the system has since been retrained, given a new data source, connected to a new workflow or pointed at a population it was never rated against, and none of that shows in the file, which now certifies a system that no longer exists. Go through it row by row — is the rating still right, did the mitigation survive the change, has a new use opened a harm nobody rated — and retest the measures the change actually touched rather than carrying forward a result from the old version. Record the outcome against every row, with the reviewer and the date, and carry the re-ratings into the register in the same pass. Attach the review record.

evidenceHint.en: Risk-file review record: the outcome against each row (unchanged, re-rated, closed, newly opened), the mitigations retested with their results, and the reviewer and date of the pass

text.en: Trigger the pass on the planned interval and on every system change.
Read each row and decide whether its rating still holds.
Retest the mitigations the change or the interval has put in doubt.
Open rows for harms the new use or population introduces.
Record the outcome per row with the reviewer named and dated.

templates.title: Training, validation and testing data governance
templates.description: Implements Art.10: govern the training, validation and testing data sets a high-risk AI system is built on — what each set is, where it came from, how it was prepared and labelled, and whether it is relevant to and representative of the people and setting the system is used in, with bias examined against the attributes that matter and every gap found recorded and acted on.

title.en: Inventory the training, validation and testing data sets the system was built on

description.en: List every data set the system learns from or is measured against, one row per set, and record where it came from, how it was collected, the version actually used, and whether it trains, validates or tests. Keep the three roles on separate rows even where one source feeds all three, because a set quietly serving as both training and test data makes every later quality claim unfalsifiable. Where a set arrived from a vendor or a public repository, record the licence position and what the supplier states about its collection. Without this list nobody can say which data the system learned from, and the measurements below have no population to run over. Attach the inventory, dated at the point it was compiled.

evidenceHint.en: Dated data set inventory: one row per set giving source, collection process, version identifier, licence position and the split it serves

text.en: List every data set used to train, validate or test the system.
Record where each set came from and how it was collected.
Give one row to each split a source feeds, not one row per source.
Record the version identifier and date of the copy actually used.
Note the licence position for every externally sourced data set.
Mark any set whose origin the records held cannot establish.

title.en: Define the intended population and the countable criteria that make a data set representative of it

description.en: Write down who the system is intended to be used on and in which geographical, contextual, behavioural and functional setting, then turn that description into attributes somebody can count — age bands, languages, regions, device types, case mixes, whatever the intended purpose makes material — with the share each should hold and the tolerance around it. Name separately the attributes where under-representation would fall on people's health, safety or rights, because those are the ones the bias examination must cover. Written down first, representativeness is measurable; left unwritten it is an opinion, and every data set passes. Agree the criteria with legal counsel and the engineering team, and attach them.

evidenceHint.en: Representativeness criteria: the intended population and setting, the countable attributes derived from it, the expected share and tolerance for each, and the attributes flagged as rights-sensitive

text.en: State the intended purpose and the people the system will be used on.
Describe the geographical, contextual and behavioural setting of use.
Turn the population description into attributes that can be counted.
Set the expected share and the tolerance for each attribute.
Flag the attributes where under-representation would affect rights.

title.en: Record the preparation, labelling and annotation each data set went through

description.en: For every set in the inventory, write down what was done to the raw data before it was used: cleaning rules, de-duplication, outlier and missing-value handling, aggregation, enrichment and any synthetic augmentation, together with the labelling step — the instructions annotators worked to and how disagreement between them was settled. Record the assumptions the preparation rests on, such as what a label is taken to mean or what a blank field is taken to indicate. A cleaning rule that silently drops a minority case is invisible in the finished set and plain here, which is the reason this record is kept separately from the data. Attach the preparation record for each set.

evidenceHint.en: Per-set preparation record covering cleaning, de-duplication, aggregation and augmentation steps, the annotation instructions issued, and the assumptions the preparation rests on

text.en: Write down each cleaning and de-duplication rule applied to the set.
Record how missing values and outliers were handled.
Attach the instructions the annotators or labellers worked to.
State how disagreement between annotators was resolved.
Record the assumptions the labels and the preparation rest on.
Note any synthetic or augmented data added and its share of the set.

title.en: Measure each data set version against the criteria and examine it for bias before it is used

description.en: Before a data set version trains or evaluates the system, count it attribute by attribute against the representativeness criteria, and examine the rights-sensitive attributes for bias in two directions: how the records are distributed across groups, and how the labels are distributed within each group — a set can be balanced on its inputs and skewed in what it was told they mean. Record every deviation with the cause found and what was done about it: reweighting, targeted collection, narrowing the population the system is offered for, or an accepted shortcoming with the reason it is acceptable. Errors and gaps found in the data belong in the same record. Attach the measurement record for each data set version used in the period.

evidenceHint.en: Measurement record per data set version: measured share against each attribute's tolerance, bias examination results by group, and the deviation, cause and action recorded for each finding

text.en: Count the set against each attribute's expected share and tolerance.
Compare the label distribution across the rights-sensitive groups.
Record every deviation from tolerance with the cause found.
Record the action taken for each deviation, or why none was taken.
Log the errors, gaps and shortcomings the examination surfaced.
Hold the record against the data set version it was run on.

title.en: Trace the model now in production back to the exact data set versions behind it

description.en: Registers age faster than models do. A corpus gets swapped in after the record was signed, a refresh runs on a schedule nobody documented, a supplier ships a replacement extract that never went through the quality gate — and the governance paperwork now describes a system that stopped existing months ago. This review pulls the lineage the build pipeline actually emitted and holds it against what the record claims, so a divergence is found by the organisation rather than by an authority reading a file that no longer matches the model in the field. Skip it and every downstream statement about representativeness, bias and provenance rests on an inventory nobody has re-tested since the day it was written, with no way to tell an honest refresh from an unrecorded substitution.

evidenceHint.en: Lineage reconciliation record for the current release: each registered set beside the version identifier the build actually used, every mismatch dated and explained, plus the corrective actions raised against named owners.

text.en: Pull from the build pipeline the data set identifiers, versions and checksums that produced the release now serving traffic.
Place that lineage beside the register entry for the same control period and flag every pair that does not agree.
For each flagged pair, obtain the storage or ticket history that dates the swap, refresh or re-extract and names who made it.
Challenge any corpus that arrived from a supplier or an upstream team with no evidence it cleared the quality gate.
Write each divergence into the record with its effect on the representativeness and bias conclusions already signed off.
Raise a corrective action wherever the shipped build rests on material the register cannot account for.

templates.title: Annex IV technical documentation
templates.description: Implements Art.11: draw up the Annex IV technical documentation demonstrating conformity before the high-risk system is placed on the market, and keep that dossier describing the version actually in the field.

title.en: Map every Annex IV heading to the document and named author that will answer it

description.en: Most of the material the dossier needs already exists somewhere in the organisation — an architecture note, a validation report, a risk file — scattered across teams that do not know a technical documentation file exists. Go heading by heading and record which document answers each one today, who owns that document and where it is held, and mark the headings nothing answers at all. A heading with no named source is the finding this task exists to surface: it is the section that gets written the night before an assessment, or never. Attach the map, dated at the point it was compiled.

evidenceHint.en: Annex IV heading-to-source map: one row per heading giving the document that answers it, its owner and where it is held, with unanswered headings marked

text.en: List the Annex IV headings as rows of one working map.
Name the document that answers each heading today.
Record the owner of each source and where it is held.
Mark every heading no existing document answers.
Agree a writer for each unanswered heading with their team.

title.en: Write the general description sections against the build being placed on the market

description.en: These are the sections nobody outside engineering can supply: what the system is for, which uses are ruled out, how it is put together, what it runs on, and exactly which version of model, code and data the description refers to. Write them against the build that is actually going to ship rather than the design as it was pitched, and pin every component to a version identifier — a dossier that describes 'the model' without saying which one cannot be checked against anything afterwards, and reads as complete while certifying nothing. Attach the drafted sections with those identifiers.

evidenceHint.en: Drafted general-description sections of the technical documentation, carrying the version identifiers of model, code, data and runtime they describe

text.en: State the intended purpose and the uses ruled out.
Describe the components, interfaces and how they connect.
Record the model, code and data versions described.
Name the hardware and runtime the released build needs.
Have the build owner read the draft back against the build.

title.en: Assemble the risk, data-governance and testing records into the dossier by dated reference

description.en: The dossier does not redo work done elsewhere, it points at it — and a pointer reading 'see the validation report' is worthless the moment three validation reports exist. Bring in each record the documentation relies on with its title, version and date, and keep a copy wherever the dossier is kept so the reference survives the source team reorganising its drive. Where a cited record does not exist yet, write it down as a gap instead of citing an intention, because an unresolvable citation is indistinguishable from a satisfied one on the page. Attach the reference list with the held copies.

evidenceHint.en: Dossier reference list naming each cited record with its version and date, the copies held alongside the dossier, and every unresolved citation recorded as a gap

text.en: List the records the documentation relies on.
Give each reference a title, version and date.
Store a copy of every cited record with the dossier.
Record as a gap any citation with no record behind it.
Open each citation and confirm it resolves to that copy.

title.en: Revise the dossier sections that each deployed change has made untrue

description.en: A high-risk system keeps moving once it is in service: a model retrained on fresh data, a threshold tuned, a new input source wired in, a guardrail relaxed. The documentation drawn up before the system reached buyers describes none of that. Treat every change that reaches production as carrying a documentation consequence - decide which headings it falsifies, rewrite them against the build now running, and date the rewrite so the currency of the file is readable at a glance. Skip this and the dossier degrades quietly: nothing fails and nothing alerts, and the organisation learns only under inspection that its conformity case rests on a description of a system it stopped running months ago.

evidenceHint.en: Dossier revision log for the period: one row per production change giving the change reference, the date, the headings rewritten, and where the superseded text is retrievable.

text.en: Put the documentation owner on the change-advisory and model-release distribution list.
For each production change, list the Annex IV headings whose text it falsifies.
Rewrite those headings against the build now running, dating each rewrite.
Keep the superseded text retrievable so an inspector can replay what changed and when.
Re-read the untouched headings each quarter to catch drift no change ticket named.

title.en: Re-check the dossier against the system in the field and name the headings it no longer answers

description.en: Take the dossier heading by heading with somebody who did not write it and compare what it claims against the system as it currently runs — the version deployed, the data it now takes, the performance it now reports, the oversight actually available to operators. Read the change log beside the releases that shipped, because the failure this catches is a release that skipped the documentation step and left a file that still looks complete. Mark each heading accurate, amended or gapped, carry the amendments in during the same pass, and give every gap an owner and a date. Attach the review record.

evidenceHint.en: Dossier review record: the outcome against every Annex IV heading, the amendments made in the pass, and each gap with its owner and date

text.en: Compare each heading against the deployed version.
Read the change log against the releases that shipped.
Mark each heading accurate, amended or gapped.
Carry the amendments into the dossier in this pass.
Give every gap recorded an owner and a date.

templates.title: Automatic event logging and record-keeping
templates.description: Implements Art.12: the high-risk AI system records its own operation automatically, so a past run can be reconstructed from the entries it emitted rather than from what anybody remembers. Covers which events are recorded and with what fields, where the entries are kept and how they are protected, whether the recording is still happening, and whether an output can actually be traced back through them.

title.en: Define the events the system records automatically and the fields each entry carries

description.en: Work through the system's intended purpose and decide which moments of its operation have to leave a trace: the start and end of each period of use, the input presented, the model version and configuration that served it, the output returned, and any person who reviewed or overrode it. Write the decision down as a schedule of event types with the fields each one carries. Without it engineering logs whatever was convenient at the time, and the first question an investigator asks turns out to be the one field nobody recorded. Attach the specification, dated, with the reasoning for anything deliberately left out.

evidenceHint.en: Dated logging specification listing each event type, the fields it carries, and the exclusions with the reasoning for each

text.en: Walk the operational flow and mark every point where the system acts on an input.
Name the event type the system emits at each of those points.
List the fields each event carries, including timestamp, version and actor.
Record why any point is deliberately left unlogged and what compensates for it.

title.en: Build the logging into the system so entries are emitted by the code path itself

description.en: Implement the specified events inside the system rather than around it, so the entry is written by the same code path that performs the action and an operator cannot complete a run without one appearing. Where a component can return a result on a branch that emits nothing, such as a cached answer, a fallback model or a timeout path, that branch is what makes the whole log untrustworthy, because the absence of an entry then means nothing at all. Attach the change record showing each event type wired to its emitting path together with the branch review that found the silent ones.

evidenceHint.en: Change record mapping every specified event type to the code path that emits it, with the branch review listing the silent paths closed

text.en: Wire each specified event type to the code path that performs the action.
Trace every return branch, including cache hits, fallbacks and timeouts.
Close the branches that can return a result while emitting no entry.
Run the system end to end and confirm each expected entry appears.

title.en: Set the retention period, storage and tamper protection for the generated entries

description.en: Decide how long the automatically generated entries are kept, where they are written, and what stops them being altered or quietly dropped. A store that can be edited after the fact traces nothing, and one rotated away after a fortnight cannot answer a question raised a year later. Set the period against how long the system stays in service and how late a problem with its output could surface, restrict who may write to or delete from the store, and make the deletion of an entry an event in its own right. Attach the configuration as applied, not as proposed.

evidenceHint.en: Applied retention and access configuration for the log store, showing the period held, the write and delete rights, and the alerting on deletion

text.en: Set the retention period against the system's service life and use.
Configure the store entries are written to and who may read it.
Restrict alteration and deletion rights to named administrators.
Make deletion and log-store configuration changes raise a record of their own.
Confirm the applied settings match the specification rather than the proposal.

title.en: Monitor the log stream for gaps and record every period when entries stopped arriving

description.en: Automatic logging fails silently: the system carries on serving output while the entries stop, and nobody notices until somebody goes looking for a run that was never recorded. Watch the arrival of entries against expected volume for every deployed instance, raise the gaps as they happen, and keep one row per gap giving its start and end, what the system was doing in the interval, and whether the missing entries could be reconstructed. Attach the period's gap register together with the volume figures it was derived from.

evidenceHint.en: Log gap register for the period, one row per interruption with its duration, the runs that fell inside it and the recovery outcome, alongside the arrival-volume figures

text.en: Compare entries received against expected volume for each instance.
Raise an alert when a stream stops or drops below its expected rate.
Record each gap with its start, end and the runs that fell inside it.
Record whether the missing entries were recovered or are lost for good.

title.en: Trace a sample of past outputs back through the logs to the run that produced them

description.en: Take outputs the system produced earlier in the period, including one from near the far end of the retention window, and reconstruct each from the entries alone: which input was presented, which model version answered it, when, and who saw or overrode the result. This is the only check that shows whether the recording is traceable rather than merely present, and what it usually finds is a field that was never captured or a correlation identifier that changes between components. Rate each reconstruction and carry the gaps back into the logging specification.

evidenceHint.en: Traceability test record naming each sampled output, whether the run could be reconstructed, the cause where it could not, and the specification changes raised

text.en: Select sample outputs spread across the period and the retention window.
Reconstruct each run from the log entries alone, using no other source.
Rate each reconstruction complete, partial or impossible with its cause.
Raise the missing fields and broken identifiers as specification changes.

templates.title: Transparency and instructions for use
templates.description: Implements Art.13: make the system's operation intelligible to the organisation deploying it, and hand that organisation instructions for use stating the intended purpose, the performance the system was tested to, the conditions under which its output should not be relied on, and what it needs to keep running correctly.

title.en: Map every output a deploying organisation acts on to the reading it must support

description.en: Take each screen, export, API field and alert a deploying organisation receives and write down what a professional user there is expected to conclude from it and then do: approve, escalate, reject, leave alone. Record beside each one the units, the range and what the figure is actually about, because a score shown without its subject and scale is read as certainty by whoever has to act on it. Where nobody can say what a field means without asking the team that built it, mark that field, because it is the transparency gap this control exists to close and a documentation review will never surface it. Attach the output map.

evidenceHint.en: Output interpretation map: one row per screen, export, field or alert giving its meaning, units and scale, the decision it feeds, and the entries nobody could explain

text.en: List every screen, export, API field and alert the deployer receives.
Record what a professional user is meant to conclude from each one.
Write down the units, scale and subject behind every figure shown.
Mark each field nobody can explain without asking the build team.

title.en: Write the instructions for use handed to the deploying organisation

description.en: Produce the document that goes to the deployer with the system, carrying the things they cannot work out for themselves: the intended purpose and the users it is built for, the accuracy and robustness figures with the measure and the population they were obtained on, the circumstances known to make the output misleading, what the system expects of input data and what it rejects, the oversight measures it offers the deployer, the resources it needs, its expected service life and its upkeep. A deployer without this operates the system outside the envelope it was tested on and has no way of knowing. Attach the issued document with its version and date.

evidenceHint.en: Versioned instructions-for-use document covering intended purpose, tested performance and its population, out-of-envelope conditions, input expectations, oversight measures available and upkeep needs

text.en: State the intended purpose and the users the system is built for.
Give the accuracy figures with the population they were measured on.
Name the conditions under which the output should not be relied on.
Specify the input data the system expects and what it rejects.
Describe the resources, service life and upkeep the system needs.
Version and date the document before it leaves the organisation.

title.en: Build the limits of each output into the surface the deploying organisation reads

description.en: Put the caveat where the decision is taken rather than in a document nobody opens at the moment of use: show the model version and the currency of the data behind the output, present the uncertainty next to the figure instead of below it, say plainly when a case falls outside the population the system was tested on, and add one line on what the output does not mean. Instructions alone leave a professional user reading a bare number in a hurry. Attach the reworked surfaces as the deployer's staff now see them.

evidenceHint.en: Before-and-after capture of each output surface showing the model version, data currency, uncertainty and out-of-scope notice now presented in place

text.en: Show the model version and the data date beside each output.
Present the uncertainty next to the figure it belongs to.
Flag any case that falls outside the tested population.
Add a plain line stating what the output does not mean.
Capture each surface as the deployer's staff now see it.

title.en: Reconcile the edition of instructions for use each deployer holds against the current release

description.en: Take the register of deployers and establish, for each one, which edition of its instructions for use it is actually working from — the revision it received, not the latest revision that exists. Set that against the edition current for the system as it runs today, single out every deployer left on an earlier one, send them what is current now, and get a dated confirmation back from a named recipient. Where something has changed since their revision in how an output is meant to be interpreted, or in what the system must not be used for, spell that out in the covering note instead of leaving it to be noticed. Skip the pass and a deployer goes on reading live output against guidance the system has outgrown, while the provider cannot show who was told what, or when. Attach the reconciliation for the period.

evidenceHint.en: Distribution reconciliation for the period: every deployer, the revision it was working from, the one current today, the gap found, the covering note sent and the dated confirmation of receipt

text.en: List every deployer of the system and the revision each was last sent.
Set each deployer's revision against the edition current today.
Single out the deployers left on an earlier revision.
Send what is current now to each one, with a covering note naming what changed.
Get a dated confirmation back from a named recipient at each deployer.

title.en: Test whether the deployer's own operators can read the output from the instructions alone

description.en: Sit with the people who actually operate the system at a deploying organisation, give them real outputs and the instructions and nothing else, and ask what each one means and what they would do next. Record every wrong reading, every question they had to escalate to reach an answer, and every part of the document they could not find. The document is clear to its authors by construction, so the only evidence that it is intelligible comes from people who did not write it. Raise a revision against each gap and attach the test record with those revisions.

evidenceHint.en: Comprehension test record naming the participants, the outputs shown, every misreading and unanswered question, and the instruction revisions raised from them

text.en: Select operators at the deployer who use the output routinely.
Give them real outputs and the instructions and nothing else.
Ask what each output means and what they would do next.
Record every misreading and every question they escalated.
Raise an instruction revision for each gap the session exposed.

templates.title: Human oversight design and operator competence
templates.description: Implements Art.14: build each high-risk AI system so a named person can follow what it is doing, read its output for what it is worth, and halt or overturn it while it runs — and put people in that seat who have the competence and the authority to use it.

title.en: Identify every point in a high-risk system's operation where a person must be able to step in

description.en: Walk each high-risk system output by output and mark the moments where a wrong result reaches somebody before any person has looked at it: the decision it feeds, who is exposed to it, and how long there is to act. Without this map, oversight gets designed against an architecture diagram rather than against the places the system can actually cause harm, and the controls end up on screens no operator ever opens. Attach the map, dated, one row per intervention point.

evidenceHint.en: Intervention-point map, one row per output: the decision it feeds, who is exposed to it, the window available for acting, and the oversight point chosen

text.en: List each output the system produces and what happens to it next.
Name the person or team an output reaches before any human check.
Record how long there is between an output and its effect landing.
Mark the points where intervention must be possible, and say why there.
Date the map and circulate it to the teams that run the system.

title.en: Build the halt, override and disregard controls into the running system

description.en: Put three distinct capabilities in front of the person holding each oversight seat: stop the operation, replace an output with their own decision, and proceed without the output while recording that they did. Each must work from where that person actually sits, with no deployment, ticket or engineer in the path — an override that needs a release is not an override, and a stop control on a page the operator never opens is decoration. Attach the interface capture and the change record.

evidenceHint.en: Interface capture and change record for each intervention point, naming the control fitted there and the measured effect it had on a live run

text.en: Add a halt control reachable from the operator's own screen.
Let the assigned person replace an output with their own decision.
Record a disregarded output as an outcome rather than as a gap.
Measure the time from pressing halt to the operation stopping.
Define the state the system is left in after a halt, and check it.

title.en: Define the competence, authority and two-person confirmation each oversight seat carries

description.en: For every intervention point, write down who holds the seat, what they must understand before they take it — the system's known limits, the cases where it is confidently wrong, how to read an output together with whatever confidence is attached to it — and what they may do without asking anyone's permission. Authority is the half usually missing: a person who must escalate before stopping the system does not oversee it. Where an output identifies a person biometrically, record that nothing acts on it until two competent people have separately confirmed it. Attach the assignment record.

evidenceHint.en: Oversight assignment record: the named holder and deputy for each seat, the competence required, the authority granted without escalation, and the outputs needing two-person confirmation

text.en: Name the person holding each oversight seat, and their deputy.
Write down what the holder must know about the system's limits.
State what the holder may halt or overturn without escalating.
Mark the outputs that need two people to confirm before any action.
Have the accountable manager sign and date the assignment record.

title.en: Record every halt, override and disregarded output with the reason the overseer gave

description.en: Keep one entry per intervention carrying who acted, which system and output, what they did, the reason in their own words, and what followed for the decision behind it. The machine's event log can show that an output was not acted on; only this entry says why a person judged it wrong, and that reasoning is what tells the provider whether the system or the oversight is the thing failing. Report the period's interventions beside the number of outputs the system produced, so the two are read together. Attach the intervention record for the period.

evidenceHint.en: Oversight intervention record for the period: one entry per halt, override or disregarded output with overseer, timestamp, stated reason and outcome, beside the total output count

text.en: Capture the overseer, the system and the output acted on.
Record the reason the person gave, in their own words.
Note what followed for the decision the output was feeding.
Report the interventions beside the period's total output count.

title.en: Test that an assigned overseer can still halt the system and that an override holds

description.en: Take each system in turn and have the person actually holding the seat — not an engineer standing in for them — halt it, override one output and disregard another, on a live or rehearsed run. Time each act to its effect, and follow the overridden output downstream to confirm the original did not travel on regardless. Read the period's intervention record in the same pass: a system producing thousands of outputs that nobody ever questioned is a finding about over-reliance, not a clean result. Record every failure with its correction and the date that correction lands.

evidenceHint.en: Oversight exercise record naming who performed each test, the measured time from act to effect, the downstream result of the overridden output, and each failure with its correction and date

text.en: Have the seat holder, not a stand-in, exercise each control.
Time each intervention from the act to its effect on the system.
Follow an overridden output downstream to confirm it was replaced.
Read the period's intervention count against the outputs produced.
Record each failure with its correction and the date it lands.

templates.title: Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
templates.description: Implements Art.15: state what the system's accuracy actually is and under what conditions it was measured, hold that level across the system's whole life, and keep it holding when an input falls outside what was tested, when a component it depends on fails, and when someone sets out to poison its training data, tamper with its artefacts or craft inputs that flip its output.

title.en: Define the accuracy metric and the level the system is declared to meet

description.en: Pick the metric that reflects what the system is actually used for, and state the minimum level claimed for it, the data it was measured on, the conditions of that measurement and the ground truth it was scored against. One headline figure hides the failure that matters, so break the level down by the output classes and the populations the system runs on. Without this, the declared level can be met and missed at the same time and nobody can tell which, and every later measurement has nothing to be compared with. Attach the performance declaration.

evidenceHint.en: Performance declaration sheet: metric per output class and population, the level claimed for each, the measurement conditions and the named ground-truth source

text.en: Name the metric that reflects each output the system produces.
State the minimum level claimed for each of those metrics.
Record the data set and the conditions each level was measured under.
Break the measured level down by the populations the system runs on.
Name the ground truth every measurement is scored against.

title.en: Configure the fallback behaviour for uncertain inputs and failed components

description.en: Decide what the system does at its edges: when an input falls outside the range it was tested on, when a dependency it needs is unavailable or returning nonsense, and when its own confidence sits below the level at which the declared accuracy holds — abstain, fall back to a safe default, hand off, or stop. Decide separately whether its own outputs may re-enter training, because a system learning from its own answers drifts away from its declared level with no single event to point at. Undefined edge behaviour does not produce an error; it produces a confident wrong answer that looks like every right one. Attach the fallback and redundancy design.

evidenceHint.en: Fallback and redundancy design: the confidence and out-of-range thresholds, the action taken at each, the safe state per dependency failure, and the rule for outputs re-entering training

text.en: Set the confidence threshold below which the system abstains.
Define what happens to inputs outside the range it was tested on.
Specify the safe state each dependency failure falls back to.
Decide whether the system's own outputs may re-enter training.
Exercise each fallback path under the condition it names.

title.en: Implement the protections against data poisoning, model tampering and adversarial input

description.en: Name the routes by which someone could change what the system does without changing what it claims to do — poisoned training or fine-tuning data, a swapped or altered model artefact, crafted inputs that flip an output, and extraction queries that lift the model or its training data back out — then put a named control against each: provenance and integrity checks on training data, signed and version-pinned artefacts, restricted write access to the pipeline that produces them, validation and rate limiting at the inference boundary. This class of compromise leaves the system running and answering, which is exactly why it goes unnoticed. Attach the mapping of route to control.

evidenceHint.en: Attack-route mapping: each route by which model behaviour could be altered against the control covering it, with the artefact signing, pipeline access and inference-boundary settings in force

text.en: List the routes by which the model's behaviour could be altered.
Sign and version-pin every model artefact that gets deployed.
Restrict write access to the training and fine-tuning data stores.
Validate and rate-limit the inputs reaching the inference boundary.
Record which control covers each route on the list.

title.en: Monitor production accuracy against the declared threshold

description.en: Accuracy proven once before deployment does not hold: input populations drift, upstream data sources change, and a model can decay in service without a line of code being touched. Without a standing measurement cycle and an agreed trigger point, that decay first shows up as a user complaint or a supervisory question rather than as an internal reading, and the provider has nothing to show that real-world performance still matches what was stated in the instructions for use. The measurement also has to bite: a reading below the threshold must open remediation, not simply be filed.

evidenceHint.en: Dated in-service performance monitoring record, one entry per measurement period, giving the sample drawn, the figure scored, the comparison verdict and any deviation ticket raised.

text.en: Draw the period's live predictions together with their confirmed outcomes from the serving records.
Score that sample using the metric fixed at scoping, and note the sample size behind the figure.
Compare the figure with the threshold held in the technical documentation, and mark any shortfall.
Open a deviation ticket, notify the deployment owner and set a remediation date whenever the figure falls short.
File the figure, the comparison and the action taken in the dated monitoring record.

title.en: Retest the fault and attack cases before each release of the system

description.en: Keep a standing set of cases — the adversarial inputs, the injected component faults, the out-of-range inputs, the extraction attempts — and run the whole set against the release candidate, comparing each result with the same case's result last time. Robustness and attack resistance decay silently: a retrain, a dependency upgrade or a threshold change can remove a protection while every functional test stays green, so the movement between runs is the signal, not the pass mark. Assign an owner to any case whose outcome moved the wrong way before the release goes out. Attach the retest report.

evidenceHint.en: Robustness and security retest report: every fault and attack case with its result, the change since the previous run, and the owner of each regression

text.en: Assemble the fault and attack cases the system is tested against.
Run every case against the release candidate build.
Compare each result with the same case's previous result.
Record any case whose outcome moved in the wrong direction.
Assign an owner to every regression before the release goes out.

templates.title: Provider conformity: assessment, CE marking, declaration and registration
templates.description: Implements Art.16: the organisation acts as the provider placing a high-risk AI system on the market — it establishes where it holds the provider role, has each system version assessed for conformity, issues and signs the EU declaration of conformity, carries the CE marking and its own identity on what ships, and registers the system in the EU database before it goes out.

title.en: Determine which high-risk systems the organisation places on the market as provider

description.en: Go product by product and decide where the organisation actually sits. It is the provider of a system it develops and puts on the market under its own name or trademark, and it becomes the provider of somebody else's system if it rebrands that system or changes what it is intended to do. Systems the organisation only runs for its own purposes belong to the deployer control, not this one, and a system filed in the wrong column here either gets a declaration nobody owed or none where one was due. For each system the organisation does provide, record the high-risk use case relied on and whether the assessment runs on internal control or needs a notified body, because that answer sets the lead time for everything below. Attach the provider-role determination with the reasoning recorded per system.

evidenceHint.en: Provider-role determination: one row per AI system giving the role held, the reasoning, the high-risk classification relied on and the assessment route chosen

text.en: List every AI system the organisation ships, sells or hosts for other organisations.
Mark each one as provider, deployer or both, with the reasoning written down.
Flag any third-party system the organisation rebrands or repurposes as its own.
Record the high-risk use case each provided system is classified under.
Decide internal control or notified body per system, and note the lead time it implies.

title.en: Conduct the conformity assessment for each provided system and record the version it cleared

description.en: Run the assessment route chosen for the system and write down what was actually examined: the technical documentation reference it rests on, who performed the assessment, the dates it ran, the notified body and certificate reference where one is involved, and the exact system version and model release that passed. An assessment recorded against a product name rather than a version cannot answer the one question an authority asks later — whether the thing on the market is the thing that was assessed. Hold open findings as blocking until each is closed, because placing a system before it cleared is not something a later fix repairs. Attach the assessment record for each system version.

evidenceHint.en: Conformity assessment record per system version: route followed, documentation cited, assessor and dates, notified body certificate where applicable, and the clearance decision

text.en: Fix the system version and model release the assessment covers.
Cite the technical documentation the assessment is carried out against.
Run the chosen route and record who performed each part of it.
Record the notified body and certificate reference where one applies.
List open findings and withhold clearance until every one is closed.

title.en: Issue a signed EU declaration of conformity naming each cleared system version

description.en: Draw up the declaration for every system version the assessment cleared: name the system and its version, identify the organisation as provider with its contact details, state the requirements and standards the declaration is made against, and have it signed by somebody authorised to bind the organisation. An unsigned draft sitting in a folder is not a declaration, and a declaration written once and never re-issued quietly stops covering the version customers are actually running. Keep each declaration retrievable next to the assessment record it rests on, so the pair can be produced together on request. Attach the signed declaration for each system version.

evidenceHint.en: One EU declaration of conformity held per cleared system version, each naming its signatory and citing the assessment record it rests on

text.en: Draft one declaration per system version the assessment cleared.
Name the provider, the system and the exact version it covers.
State the requirements and standards it is declared against.
Obtain the signature of somebody authorised to bind the organisation.
Store the signed declaration alongside the assessment record it cites.

title.en: Register each system in the EU database and confirm its CE marking before it is placed on the market

description.en: Every time a system or a new version goes out, run the same gate before it leaves: the EU database entry exists and its details match what is shipping, the CE marking is present on the system or its packaging and accompanying documentation, and the provider's name and contact address travel with it. Record the entry identifier, the date registered and the date the version was placed on the market, one row per system version. A registration made after shipping cannot be backdated, and a marking carried over unchanged from a previous release points customers and authorities at a declaration that no longer describes the product. Attach the placing-on-the-market record for the period.

evidenceHint.en: Placing-on-the-market record for the period: one row per system version with its EU database entry identifier, registration date, CE marking confirmation and the date it was placed on the market

text.en: Create or update the EU database entry for the system version.
Check the registered details match the version about to ship.
Confirm the CE marking appears on the system or its packaging.
Confirm the provider's name and contact address ship with it.
Record the entry identifier and the date placed on the market.

title.en: Reconcile declarations, markings and registrations against the systems actually on the market

description.en: Take an independent view of what the organisation currently has on the market — the price list, the release log, the customer-facing catalogue — and match it in both directions against the declarations, marking confirmations and database entries held. Three failures leave every individual record looking healthy: a version shipped since the last declaration was signed, a change to intended purpose or performance large enough that the cleared assessment no longer describes the system, and an entry still registered for a product withdrawn from sale. Record each mismatch with an owner, the decision taken — re-assess, re-declare, correct the entry, withdraw — and the date it was closed. Attach the reconciliation with its mismatch list.

evidenceHint.en: Reconciliation record matching each system on the market to its declaration, marking and registration entry, listing mismatches, decisions and closing dates

text.en: Take an independent list of the systems currently on the market.
Match each system to a signed declaration and a registration entry.
Match each declaration and database entry back to a live system.
Flag versions changed since the assessment that cleared them.
Record every mismatch with an owner, a decision and a closing date.

templates.title: Quality management system
templates.description: Implements Art.17: operate a written quality management system across the organisation that places high-risk AI on the market — its agreed scope, an accountability framework naming who answers for each part, the indexed and versioned procedure set covering design control, development and quality assurance, examination and validation, data management, post-market monitoring, incident reporting, communication with authorities, record-keeping and resource supply, the records those procedures produce, and the internal audit and management review that keep them in force. This is the provider's system of working, not the risk work done on any one AI system.

title.en: Scope the quality management system to every product line and site that ships high-risk AI

description.en: Write down which legal entities, development sites, product lines and outsourced parties the quality system governs, and which are deliberately outside it. A quality system scoped implicitly ends up meaning whichever team wrote it: a contract development house training a model, or a second office shipping under the same provider name, sits outside every procedure while the paperwork still reads as complete. Name the excluded parts and the reason each is excluded, because an unexplained gap is indistinguishable from an oversight. Attach the scope statement with the date it was agreed and who agreed it.

evidenceHint.en: Dated quality management system scope statement listing the entities, sites, product lines and outsourced parties governed, with each exclusion and its stated reason

text.en: List the legal entities and development sites that build or ship high-risk AI.
Name the product lines each site places on the market under the provider's name.
Record every outsourced party that performs a step of design, development or testing.
Mark each item as inside or outside the quality system and give the reason.
Date the scope statement and record who agreed it.

title.en: Write the accountability framework naming the role answerable for each part of the quality system

description.en: Set out in writing which role carries which responsibility for the quality system: who approves a procedure, who may authorise a departure from one, who answers to the management body for the system as a whole, and who holds the same duties at each site the scope covers. Responsibility recorded as a team name is not an accountability framework — when a procedure is skipped, somebody has to be identifiable as the person who should have stopped it. Record the reporting line from each role upward, so a finding has somewhere to go. Attach the framework showing role, responsibility, approval authority and reporting line.

evidenceHint.en: Accountability framework: one row per role giving its quality-system responsibilities, its authority to approve or waive a procedure, and its reporting line to management

text.en: List the quality-system duties that need a named owner.
Name the role, not the person, accountable for each duty.
Record who may approve a procedure and who may authorise a departure.
Trace each role's reporting line up to the management body.
Have management adopt the framework and record the date.

title.en: Catalogue the written procedures the quality system holds, with the owner and version of each

description.en: Build the index of the procedures the quality system is actually made of — design and design control, development and quality assurance, examination and validation, data management, post-market monitoring, incident reporting, communication with authorities, record-keeping and resource supply — and record for each its document reference, current version, owner and approval date. Without the index a missing procedure leaves no trace, because absence looks exactly like nothing; with it, an empty row is visible to anyone who opens the file. Where a required procedure does not exist yet, keep its row and mark it outstanding rather than omitting it. Attach the procedure index.

evidenceHint.en: Quality-system procedure index listing each procedure with its document reference, current version, owner, approval date and any row marked outstanding

text.en: List the procedures the quality system is required to hold.
Record the document reference and current version for each one.
Name the owner and the date the current version was approved.
Mark any required procedure that does not yet exist as outstanding.
Publish the index where every team in scope can reach it.

title.en: Log every departure from a quality procedure and the corrective action closed against it

description.en: Through the period, record each occasion a quality procedure was not followed — a design review skipped to hold a release date, a validation signed off on partial results, a supplier step done outside the documented flow — with the date, who authorised or discovered it, and the corrective action raised. A quality system with an empty deviation log is rarely a system nobody departed from; it is usually a system nobody records against, which is the exact state this log exists to make visible. Carry each corrective action through to a closure date rather than leaving it open and unread. Attach the deviation and corrective-action log for the period.

evidenceHint.en: Deviation and corrective-action log for the period: each departure with its date, who raised it, the action taken, and its closure date or open status

text.en: Record each departure from a documented procedure as it happens.
Note who authorised or discovered it and on what date.
Raise a corrective action against every departure logged.
Record the closure date and what changed as a result.
Export the log for the period with open items still showing.

title.en: Audit the quality system against its own procedures and report where practice has diverged

description.en: Take the procedure index and test, procedure by procedure, whether the work is really done the way the document says — sample actual releases and actual records rather than asking the owners, because a procedure everybody has quietly stopped following still reads as current on the page. Record each divergence with the evidence that revealed it, the role accountable under the framework, and a due date. Put the findings in front of the management body together with the deviation log and any outstanding procedure rows, so the choice to change a procedure or enforce it is made by someone who can resource it. Attach the audit report and the minutes of that review.

evidenceHint.en: Internal quality-system audit report giving per-procedure findings, the records sampled, the accountable role and due dates, with the minuted management review that received it

text.en: Sample real releases and records against each written procedure.
Record every divergence with the evidence that revealed it.
Assign each finding to the role accountable under the framework.
Put the findings, deviation log and outstanding rows to management.
Minute the decisions taken and the dates they are due.

templates.title: Deployer operating obligations
templates.description: Implements Art.26: the organisation uses each high-risk AI system it did not build within the conditions the supplier's instructions state, assigns named people with the authority and the standing to oversee it and halt it, monitors how it behaves while in use and reports what it sees to the supplier, keeps the logs the system generates under its control, and tells the workers it is used on — the obligations that fall on the party using a system rather than the party placing it on the market.

title.en: List the AI systems the organisation deploys but did not build, and the instructions for use held for each

description.en: Deployer duties attach to systems somebody else supplied, so the first job is knowing which ones are in use and on what terms. Walk the procurement records, the software spend and the business teams themselves, and record for each system what it decides or assists with, which process it sits inside, who supplied it, and whether the instructions for use are actually in the organisation's hands — a system in daily use whose instructions nobody has ever read is the finding this task exists to surface. Where the supplier has sent nothing, ask for it and record the date of the request. Attach the deployment register.

evidenceHint.en: Deployment register: one row per AI system in use, giving the supplier, the process it sits in, the people it affects and whether the instructions for use are held

text.en: Pull the procurement and software records for systems with an AI component.
Ask each business team which AI systems they use and for what decisions.
Record the supplier, the process it sits in and the people it affects.
Note for each system whether the instructions for use are held and read.
Request the missing instructions from the supplier and date the request.

title.en: Extract the provider's operating conditions and limits into the procedure the operating team follows

description.en: Instructions for use are written for the organisation, not for the person at the screen, so turn each set into the working procedure that person actually has: the purposes the system may be used for, the input data it may be given, the conditions it must run under, the outputs that must not be acted on alone, and how long its logs are kept and who can retrieve them. Name the instruction clause beside each line, so a later reader can tell an obligation the supplier stated from a habit the team invented. Where a stated condition cannot be met with what the organisation has, record it as a gap and escalate it rather than writing a procedure that quietly ignores it. Attach the procedure for each system.

evidenceHint.en: Operating procedure per deployed system, each line citing the instruction clause it came from, with the conditions the organisation cannot meet listed separately

text.en: Read the instructions for use and list every condition they state.
Write down the permitted purposes and the input data the system may be given.
Set how long the system's logs are kept and who may retrieve them.
Cite the instruction clause behind each line of the procedure.
Record any stated condition the organisation cannot meet as a gap.

title.en: Assign named overseers to each deployed system and give them written authority to halt its use

description.en: Oversight that is nobody's job in particular is not oversight. For each deployed system name the individuals who watch its output and a deputy, cover the hours it actually runs, and put in writing that they may set aside a result or stop the system without seeking approval first — an overseer who must escalate in order to halt will not halt. Record what they were given to do the job: the training on this specific system, the access needed to see its inputs and outputs, and the time allowed for the work. Tell the workers the system will be used on, and their representatives, that it is coming and who oversees it. Attach the oversight assignment record.

evidenceHint.en: Oversight assignment record naming the overseer and deputy for each system, their written authority to halt it, the hours covered, and the training and access given

text.en: Name the overseer and a deputy for each deployed system.
Put the authority to set aside a result or halt the system in writing.
Match the oversight roster to the hours the system actually runs.
Record the training and the access each named overseer received.
Tell the affected workers and their representatives before use begins.

title.en: Monitor each deployed system against its stated conditions and report the deviations to the supplier

description.en: Monitoring here means watching a system the organisation cannot change: what is available is the output it produces, the input it is fed and the logs it writes, read against the conditions the procedure records. Each period, record what was observed, every case where the system was used outside those conditions or behaved in a way the instructions do not describe, what the overseers did about it, and which cases were reported to the supplier — and where use appeared to put people's health, safety or rights at risk, record the decision to suspend the system, who took it and when the authorities were told. Keep the logs the system generated over the same period beside the record, because the observations cannot be checked without them. Attach the monitoring record for the period.

evidenceHint.en: Monitoring record for the period: the deviations observed, what the overseers did, the notifications sent to the supplier or the authorities, any suspension decision, and the retained system logs covering the same dates

text.en: Compare the period's use against the conditions in the procedure.
Record every deviation and what the overseer did about it.
Notify the supplier of behaviour the instructions do not describe.
Record any suspension decision, who took it and who was told.
Store the logs the system generated over the same period.

title.en: Re-read each supplier's current instructions against how the system is actually being used

description.en: Two things drift apart quietly: the supplier reissues the instructions after an update, and the organisation finds new uses for a system it bought for one. Take the current instructions from the supplier rather than the copy filed at purchase, put them beside the procedure, the period's monitoring record and the oversight roster, and record for each system whether the purposes, the input data, the operating conditions, the named overseers and the log coverage still match.
