Where they do not, say which side moved: a use that has grown beyond what the supplier describes is a different problem from a procedure that is merely out of date, and the two are corrected by different people. Attach the review with its findings and the corrections made.

evidenceHint.en: Instructions-versus-practice review for each deployed system, naming the instruction version compared, every divergence found, which side moved and the correction made

text.en: Obtain the current instructions for use from each supplier.
Compare them against the procedure written for that system.
Check the purposes and input data in use are still the ones stated.
Confirm the named overseers are still in post and still trained.
Check the retained logs cover every period the system ran.
Record each divergence, which side moved and the correction made.

templates.title: Fundamental rights impact assessment
templates.description: Implements Art.27: before a high-risk AI system is put into use, the deployers the Act names assess what its use could do to the fundamental rights of the people it will be applied to — which categories and groups are affected, what harm could follow for them, who watches for that harm and how an affected person complains — then notify the result to the market surveillance authority and keep the assessment current as the deployment changes.

title.en: Identify the people and groups each high-risk deployment will affect, before it goes into use

description.en: Take each high-risk system the organisation is about to put into use and write down the decision or process it will feed, the period and frequency over which it will run, and — the part this assessment exists for — which categories of natural person the output actually lands on: applicants, claimants, patients, tenants, students, employees. Name the sub-groups inside them carrying more exposure than the average, because an assessment written about 'users' never finds the group the harm falls on. Compiled after go-live it is a formality: the deployment decisions it should have changed have already been made. Attach the affected-persons register, dated before first use.

evidenceHint.en: Affected-persons register per deployment: the process it feeds, the period and frequency of intended use, and every category and sub-group of person the output is applied to

text.en: Write down the decision or process the system will feed into.
Record the period and frequency over which it will run.
Name every category of person the output is applied to.
Mark the sub-groups more exposed than the general population.
Date the register before the system is put into use.

title.en: Assess the harm to each affected group's fundamental rights that use of the system could cause

description.en: Work group by group down the register and state what could go wrong for those people specifically — a service wrongly refused, an entitlement delayed, an outcome that falls harder on one group than another, a decision nobody can explain to the person it was made about — and how likely and how serious each would be. This is not the provider's engineering risk analysis restated: the subject is the person on the receiving end, not the failure mode inside the model. Record the reasoning beside each harm, because a rating with no reasoning cannot be challenged by anyone and cannot be re-run when the deployment moves. Attach the assessment covering every group the register names.

evidenceHint.en: Fundamental-rights impact assessment, one entry per affected group: the harm described in concrete terms, its likelihood and severity, and the reasoning recorded for each

text.en: Take each group from the affected-persons register in turn.
Describe the harm that group could suffer in concrete terms.
Rate how likely and how severe that harm would be.
Write down the reasoning that produced each rating.
Check that no group in the register is left unassessed.

title.en: Record the oversight, response and complaint arrangements protecting the people assessed

description.en: For every harm the assessment carries forward, record what the organisation will actually do about it: who inside the deployment watches for it, what that person is able to stop, override or escalate, what happens in the hours after it materialises, and how an affected person raises the matter and gets an answer back. Name the owner and the route by name rather than by function, because 'appropriate governance arrangements' commits nobody to anything on the day it is needed. A harm that is documented and has no named response is the one an affected person and an inspector both find first. Attach the measures record mapped one-to-one onto the assessed harms.

evidenceHint.en: Measures record mapping each assessed harm to its named internal owner, the oversight and response arrangement agreed for it, and the complaint route open to affected people

text.en: Take each harm carried forward from the assessment.
Name the person inside the deployment accountable for it.
State what that person can stop, override or escalate.
Write down the complaint route open to an affected person.
Confirm every assessed harm has a measure against it.

title.en: Notify the market surveillance authority of the assessment result and keep the submission proof

description.en: Once the assessment is complete, notify the market surveillance authority of its result and keep what proves it: the version submitted, the form used, the date, the person who sent it and whatever acknowledgement came back. Freeze the submitted copy rather than letting the working document drift over it, because the filing and the live assessment answer different questions later — what the authority was told, and what the organisation believes now. An assessment performed and never notified leaves the organisation carrying all of the work and none of the credit, and shows as a gap at the first inspection. Attach the submission record for every deployment notified in the period.

evidenceHint.en: Submission record per notified deployment: the frozen version of the assessment sent, the form used, the date, the submitter and any acknowledgement received

text.en: Freeze the version of the assessment being submitted.
Send it to the market surveillance authority on the form it accepts.
Record the date, the submitter and the form used.
Store the acknowledgement alongside the frozen version.
List every deployment notified during the period.

title.en: Reassess the affected groups and their harms when the use, the population or the system changes

description.en: This assessment goes stale quietly. The system is pointed at a second process, the caseload shifts to a different population, the provider ships a new version, or a measure that was written down turns out never to have been staffed — and none of those announce themselves as a change to the fundamental-rights position. Re-read the assessment against what the deployment is actually doing now, record which groups, harms and measures changed, and carry the corrections into the document in the same pass rather than logging them for a later one. Attach the dated reassessment naming the reviewer and stating what changed.

evidenceHint.en: Dated reassessment record listing each trigger examined, the affected groups, harms and measures amended as a result, and the reviewer who performed it

text.en: Compare the recorded intended use against the current use.
Check whether the affected population has shifted since filing.
Ask whether the provider has changed the system since then.
Test that each recorded measure is actually staffed.
Amend the assessment and date the reassessment record.

templates.title: Limited-risk (transparency obligations)
templates.description: Implements Art.50: tell people when they are dealing with an AI system rather than a person, and mark or label AI-generated and manipulated content so everyone who meets it can tell what it is.

title.en: Inventory every point where a person meets the AI system or content it generated

description.en: Walk the product and the public channels and record, one row each, the places where a member of the public interacts with the system (chat, voice assistant, in-app helper, phone line) and the places where output the system generated or altered reaches someone (images, audio, video, published text). For each row name who the exposed person is, whether they are told anything today, and which limb applies: interaction disclosure, content marking, or both. Systems that infer emotion or sort people into categories from biometric data belong here too, because the people exposed to them have to be told the feature is running. Without the inventory the disclosure work covers the surfaces somebody remembered, and the ones it misses are the ones nobody is watching. Attach the inventory dated at the point it was compiled.

evidenceHint.en: Dated exposure inventory: one row per interaction or content surface, naming the audience exposed to it and the disclosure that reaches them today

text.en: Walk each product surface a member of the public can reach.
Record every channel where the system speaks to a person.
Record every output type the system generates or alters.
Note any emotion-inference or biometric categorisation in use.
Mark which rows already show a disclosure today.

title.en: Write the first-contact notice that tells a person they are dealing with an AI

description.en: Draft the wording each interaction surface shows before the person's first exchange: that they are dealing with an AI system rather than a person, and how to reach a human where that route exists. Place it where it cannot be missed rather than in the terms of service, keep it visible when a conversation hands back from a human agent to the machine, and give voice and telephone channels a spoken equivalent, because a screen notice never reaches a caller. Where the system infers emotion or sorts people by biometric category, the notice tells the exposed person that feature is operating while it operates. Without it a person answers questions they would not have answered to a machine and only finds out afterwards. Attach the approved wording per surface with a capture showing where it appears.

evidenceHint.en: Approved disclosure wording for each interaction surface, with captures showing where and when the exposed person sees or hears it

text.en: Draft the wording for each interaction surface.
Add a spoken version for voice and phone channels.
Place the notice ahead of the first exchange.
Keep it visible after a handover back from a human.
Capture each surface as the person actually sees it.

title.en: Mark the output the system generates so a machine can detect it as synthetic

description.en: Attach provenance metadata or a watermark to image, audio, video and text output at the moment it is generated rather than at the moment it is published, because output leaves the system by paths nobody remembers to cover. Record for each output type which technique is used, which export, download and re-encode paths preserve it, and where it is known to be stripped — an honest list of limits is worth more than a claim of full coverage. Where no marking can be applied to a format the system emits, record that gap and what compensates for it. Without a durable mark, somebody who receives the file later has no way to establish it came from a machine, and the visible label alone disappears the first time the asset is cropped or re-shared. Attach the marking specification with the test results behind it.

evidenceHint.en: Marking specification per output type, with test results showing which export, re-encode and download paths preserve the marker and which strip it

text.en: Choose a marking technique per output format.
Apply the marker in the generation path itself.
Test whether export and re-encoding preserve it.
Record every path that strips the marker.
Write up the gaps and what compensates for them.

title.en: Log every published deepfake and AI-written item with the label the audience saw

description.en: Each time manipulated or generated content resembling real people, places or events is published, and each time AI-written text goes out to inform the public, record what was published, where, when, who cleared it and the exact visible label it carried at the point somebody consumes it — a disclosure sitting in a caption nobody scrolls to is not the same as one on the asset. Keep the item or a capture of it beside the row so the label can be checked later rather than asserted. An item that went out unlabelled is recorded as such with the correction and its date, because a register that only shows the successes tells a reviewer nothing. Attach the publication log for the period.

evidenceHint.en: Publication log for the period: one row per generated or manipulated item giving channel, date, approver, the label shown, and a capture of the item as published

text.en: Record each publication of generated or altered content.
Capture the item showing the label as published.
Name the person who cleared it for release.
Log any item that went out without a label.
Record the correction made and the date it landed.

title.en: Re-check each surface from the exposed person's side and list what no longer discloses

description.en: Take the inventory row by row and approach each surface the way an outsider does — open the chat cold, call the phone line, download a generated file, view a published item on a phone — and record what the person actually meets: a disclosure that survived the last redesign, one that has quietly moved below the fold, or none at all. Re-test the markings against the current export paths in the same pass, since a codec or library upgrade strips a watermark without anything failing anywhere. Record surfaces the inventory never knew about, which is the finding only this direction of reading produces. Carry every gap into a correction with an owner and a date. Attach the review record naming who performed it and when.

evidenceHint.en: Review record listing every surface tested, the disclosure or marking actually found, the gaps including surfaces missing from the inventory, and the correction raised for each with owner and date

text.en: Approach each inventoried surface as an outsider.
Record the disclosure the person actually meets.
Re-test markings against current export paths.
List surfaces missing from the inventory.
Raise a correction with an owner and a date.

templates.title: GPAI provider obligations: documentation, downstream information and copyright
templates.description: Implements Art.53: the baseline every provider of a general-purpose AI model owes, whatever the model's scale — technical documentation kept current per model version, the information a downstream provider needs to build on the model lawfully, a copyright policy that honours reserved rights inside the training pipeline, and a public summary of the content the model was trained on. Obligations that attach only to models carrying systemic risk are held by their own control.

title.en: Inventory every general-purpose AI model the organisation releases and the route it reaches users by

description.en: Write down each general-purpose model the organisation trains, fine-tunes substantially, or re-releases under its own name, together with how it leaves the building — hosted API, downloadable weights, a partner licence, or embedded in the organisation's own product. This register decides which obligations attach to whom: a team that believes it merely uses somebody else's model, while publishing a fine-tuned checkpoint under the company name, is a provider and nobody has told it so. Record the version and release date each row refers to, and have counsel confirm the provider call. Attach the register.

evidenceHint.en: General-purpose model register: one row per model version giving its release route, release date, named owner and the confirmed provider determination

text.en: List every model the organisation trains, fine-tunes or re-releases under its own name.
Record the release route for each model: API, weights, licence or embedded product.
Note the model version and the release date each row refers to.
Ask counsel to confirm, row by row, whether the organisation is the provider.
Name an accountable owner against each model in the register.

title.en: Compile the technical documentation held for each general-purpose model version

description.en: Build one documentation set per released model version covering how that model was built and tested: architecture and parameter count, the modalities and intended uses, the training and testing process, the compute and energy the run consumed, and the evaluation results the organisation actually obtained. It is drawn up at the release and kept current, because documentation reconstructed months later from memory and scattered notebooks is where the undocumented training run surfaces. Store it so it can be handed over on request without standing up a project to assemble it. Attach the set for every version on the market.

evidenceHint.en: Per-version model documentation set covering architecture, training and testing process, compute accounting and evaluation results, tagged with the version it describes

text.en: Record architecture, parameter count and the modalities the model handles.
Describe the training and testing process, data-preparation stages included.
Record the compute and the energy consumed by the training run.
Attach the evaluation results obtained for this particular version.
Tag the set with the model version it describes and store it for release.

title.en: Write the copyright policy that governs what the model's training pipeline may collect

description.en: State in writing which sources the training pipeline may draw on and what happens when a rights holder has reserved its rights: how crawlers read machine-readable reservations, which licensed corpora are approved and on what terms, who signs off a new source before it enters a run, and what a contracted data supplier must warrant. Then configure the collection tooling to match. A policy asserting that reservations are honoured while the crawler ignores them is worse than no policy, because it documents the gap in the organisation's own words. Attach the policy together with the configuration that enforces it.

evidenceHint.en: Copyright policy for training data, with the crawler and ingestion configuration showing how reserved rights are detected and excluded

text.en: List the source categories the training pipeline may draw data from.
Set out how machine-readable rights reservations are detected and honoured.
Name who approves a new data source before it enters a training run.
Configure the crawler to exclude sources that have reserved their rights.
Add the warranty a contracted data supplier must give on rights.

title.en: Issue the downstream integrator pack with every general-purpose model release

description.en: A provider building a product on this model cannot meet its own obligations from an API reference. At each release, send every integrating customer on record what they need: capabilities and tested limitations, intended and excluded uses, the evaluation results bearing on those uses, integration constraints, and what changed since the version they are running. Record who received which version and when, because the failure mode here is silent — an integrator left on last year's pack keeps building on behaviour the model no longer has. Attach the pack issued this period and the distribution record.

evidenceHint.en: Downstream integrator pack issued this period, with the distribution record naming each recipient, the version they received and the date

text.en: Assemble capabilities, tested limitations and excluded uses for the release.
Add the evaluation results bearing on the integrator's intended uses.
Write the change note covering what differs from the previous version.
Send the pack to every integrating provider on the distribution list.
Record recipient, version received and date against each delivery.

title.en: Reconcile the published training-content summary against the data used for the shipped model

description.en: The training-content summary is the one obligation here whose output the public can read, so drift in it is visible from outside the organisation. Take the summary as published and compare it collection by collection against the data manifest for the version actually on the market: a corpus added late in a run, a licensed source dropped, or a modality introduced by a fine-tune all leave the published text describing a model that no longer exists. Republish a dated update wherever the two disagree; where nothing has been published yet, this pass produces the first summary. Attach the comparison and the summary as it now stands.

evidenceHint.en: Summary reconciliation record listing each collection compared and every difference found, with the dated training-content summary as republished

text.en: Export the data manifest for the model version now on the market.
Compare each collection named in the summary against that manifest.
Record every source added, dropped or re-licensed since publication.
Rewrite the summary so a rights holder can recognise their material.
Republish the summary dated, keeping the previous version visible.

templates.title: Systemic-risk GPAI: evaluation, adversarial testing, incident reporting and model security
templates.description: Implements Art.55: the additional tier a general-purpose model with systemic risk carries on top of the baseline every GPAI provider owes — state-of-the-art evaluation of the model, adversarial testing of it, tracking and reporting serious incidents, and protecting the weights and the environment that trains and serves them.

title.en: Determine which general-purpose models carry systemic risk, and record what the decision rested on

description.en: Everything else in this control applies to a named list of models, so the list is the first deliverable and the one most often assumed rather than written down. Record per model the training compute, the capability evidence weighed, whether it entered the tier by designation or by the provider's own assessment, and who signed that decision. Record the models examined and left out as well, because the near misses are what an assessor asks about, and name the event that forces the question to be asked again.

evidenceHint.en: Systemic-risk determination record: one entry per general-purpose model with the compute and capability evidence, the in-or-out decision, its signatory, and the event that re-opens it

text.en: Record the training compute for each general-purpose model provided.
Gather the capability evidence that bears on the tier decision.
State for each model whether it is in the tier, and on what grounds.
List the models examined and left out, with a reason against each.
Name the event that forces the determination to be made again.

title.en: Define the evaluation protocol and the capability thresholds a systemic-risk model must clear before release

description.en: An evaluation designed after the results are in can be argued into any conclusion, so fix the protocol first: which capabilities are measured, against which benchmarks and internal test sets, at what threshold a result becomes a blocker, and what happens to the release when one is crossed. Name the standardised protocols and tooling used, so a later reader can tell a state-of-the-art evaluation from an ad-hoc one, and state who may release over a crossed threshold and on what record. Without thresholds written in advance the evaluation becomes a report nobody can fail.

evidenceHint.en: Model evaluation protocol naming the capabilities measured, the tests and tooling used, each decision threshold, and the release rule a crossed threshold triggers

text.en: List the capabilities that must be measured before a release.
Choose the benchmarks, internal test sets and tooling for each.
Set the threshold at which a result blocks the release.
Write what happens to a release when a threshold is crossed.
Agree who may approve a release over a crossed threshold.

title.en: Run adversarial testing against each systemic-risk model version and record what got through

description.en: Test the model as an attacker would rather than as the benchmark suite does: jailbreaks and prompt injection, deliberate elicitation of the capabilities the protocol calls dangerous, misuse chains that combine tools, and fine-tuning or weight-level attacks where the model is released openly. Record every attempt that succeeded with the transcript or artefact that proves it, the severity assigned, and whether it was fixed, accepted or left open at release. A campaign that reports only a pass rate cannot be acted on and shows nobody what the model does under pressure.

evidenceHint.en: Adversarial testing campaign record per model version: attempts made, each successful attack with the transcript proving it, severity, and the mitigation or accepted risk against it

text.en: Scope the campaign on the dangerous capabilities the protocol names.
Name the testers and state their independence from the build team.
Record each successful attack with the transcript that proves it.
Assign a severity and a named owner to every finding.
Record the fix, the accepted risk or the open item at release.

title.en: Track every serious incident involving a systemic-risk model from detection to the report that leaves the organisation

description.en: Keeping a register is the easy half; the half that fails is the handover from an engineer noticing something to a report leaving the building with a corrective measure attached. Record for each incident what was detected and when, how it was classified and by whom, what went to the authority and on what date, the acknowledgement received back, and what was changed in the model or its safeguards afterwards. Include the incidents downstream providers and deployers report to you, which is the route most of them will arrive by and the one no internal alert will ever raise.

evidenceHint.en: Serious-incident register for the period: detection and classification times, the outward report with its acknowledgement, and the corrective measure recorded against each incident

text.en: State what counts as a serious incident for this model.
Record the detection time and the person who raised it.
Record the classification decision and who made it.
Log the incidents downstream providers and deployers report in.
File the report, then store the acknowledgement received back.
Record the corrective measure applied to the model.

title.en: Re-verify who can reach the model weights and the training environment, and close every path that is not on the list

description.en: Cybersecurity for a systemic-risk model is about the weights and the environment that produces them, not the product wrapped around them. Pull the actual access lists for the weight stores, checkpoint buckets, training clusters, signing keys and the facilities housing that hardware, compare them against the people and services meant to hold access, and remove whatever nobody can account for. Then test the way out: attempt to copy a checkpoint by the routes an insider would use, and record whether it was blocked, alerted on, or completed unnoticed. A list reviewed on paper shows who was authorised, never who could still walk off with a copy.

evidenceHint.en: Weight-access recertification naming every principal holding access to weight stores, training clusters, signing keys and the facilities housing them, with the removals made and the egress-test result

text.en: Export the access lists for weight stores and training clusters.
Include the signing keys and physical access to the hardware.
Compare every principal against the authorised list.
Remove the access that nobody present can account for.
Attempt a checkpoint copy by the routes an insider would use.
Record whether the attempt was blocked, alerted on or unnoticed.

templates.title: Minimal-risk AI systems
templates.description: Implements Art.95: minimal-risk AI systems carry no mandatory obligations under the Act, so the work is establishing that a system genuinely belongs in this residual tier rather than assuming it, recording the classification and the reasoning behind it, deciding deliberately whether to adopt a voluntary code of conduct, and re-checking when the system changes.

title.en: Classify each AI system as minimal-risk only by ruling out the regulated tiers

description.en: Minimal-risk is what is left after the Act's regulated tiers have been excluded, so it is reached by elimination and never by assertion. Take each system in the AI inventory and work through the prohibited practices, the high-risk categories, the transparency triggers for systems people interact with, and the general-purpose model definitions, recording for each tier what made it not apply here. Without that reasoning written down a tenant has an unevidenced claim rather than a classification, and nobody later can tell whether the tier was checked or assumed. Attach the classification record with the decision-maker and date against every system.

evidenceHint.en: Dated classification record listing each system, the tiers ruled out, the ground for ruling each out, and who decided

text.en: Take the AI system inventory as the population to be classified.
Work each system against the prohibited, high-risk, transparency and general-purpose tiers in turn.
Record for every tier ruled out the specific ground that rules it out.
Name the person who made the classification and the date it was made.
Send any system whose tier is arguable to legal counsel before recording it.

title.en: Evaluate the voluntary codes of conduct available and record the adoption decision

description.en: The Act encourages codes of conduct for systems outside the regulated tiers and requires none of them, so the deliverable here is a decision taken on purpose rather than a commitment. Gather the codes that plausibly cover these systems, summarise what each would actually oblige the organisation to do, and put that to whoever can commit the organisation. Declining every code is a legitimate outcome and the one most often left unrecorded, which is how a decision nobody made gets re-litigated each year and how an unconsidered code later reads as an oversight. Attach the signed decision covering each code considered.

evidenceHint.en: Signed decision record naming the codes considered, what each would commit the organisation to, and the decision reached on each

text.en: Collect the voluntary codes of conduct that address the systems in scope.
Summarise for each code what committing to it would require in practice.
Estimate the effort and the cost of meeting each set of commitments.
Put the options to the person who can commit the organisation.
Record the decision reached on each code, adoption and declination alike.
Date and sign the record so the choice is attributable afterwards.

title.en: Map each commitment in an adopted code to the owner and the practice that delivers it

description.en: Adopting a code is voluntary, but once adopted its commitments are what the organisation now says about itself, and a public claim nobody delivers is worse than no claim at all. Break the adopted code into its individual commitments, name the person accountable for each, and name the practice or artifact that satisfies it today, marking the ones nothing currently satisfies because those are the gap between the claim and the reality. Where the previous task adopted no code, close this one with a note pointing at that decision, so nobody later asserts adherence the organisation never took on. Attach the commitment map or the note.

evidenceHint.en: Commitment map: one row per clause of the adopted code, each naming who owns it and which existing practice satisfies it, or the note recording that no code was adopted

text.en: Break the adopted code into its individual commitments, one row each.
Name the person accountable for delivering each commitment.
Name the existing practice or artifact that satisfies each commitment.
Mark the commitments that nothing currently satisfies as open gaps.
Where no code was adopted, record that and cite the decision record.

title.en: Record every change to a minimal-risk system that could move it out of the tier

description.en: A classification is true of a system as it was when it was classified, and these systems change: a new purpose, a new user group, a new data source or a model swap can carry one into a tier that does carry obligations. Attach a tier question to the change route these systems already go through, capture the changes that answer it, and re-run the classification where the change is material, recording the outcome next to the change. Without this the register slowly describes systems that no longer exist, and the tier is discovered to be wrong by somebody outside the organisation. Attach the change log for the period.

evidenceHint.en: Change log for minimal-risk systems covering the period, showing each new purpose, capability or user group, the re-check outcome and its date

text.en: Attach a tier question to the change process these systems go through.
Capture each new purpose, user group, data source or model substitution.
Re-run the tier classification wherever a captured change is material.
Record the outcome of that re-check beside the change entry itself.
Hand any system that leaves the tier to the owner of its new obligations.

title.en: Re-check the recorded minimal-risk classifications and confirm each one still holds

description.en: Changes captured one at a time miss the drift that arrives gradually and the systems whose changes never reached the change route at all, so the whole population is read again against how it is actually used today. Take each system carried as minimal-risk, compare the reasoning recorded for it against its current purpose and users, and state plainly whether the tier is confirmed or changed rather than leaving the entry untouched, since an unrevisited row and a confirmed row look identical afterwards. Attach the dated review naming every system and its outcome.

evidenceHint.en: Dated re-classification review listing every system carried as minimal-risk, whether its tier was confirmed or changed, and where each moved system went

State for each system whether the tier is confirmed or changed.
List the systems that left the tier and the tier they moved into.
Report the outcome to the owner of the AI system inventory.
